name: NEET/JEE Physics & Chemistry — by Catalyzers Institute
intro: Namaste! I'm Catalyzers Institute's tutor. I'll help you master NEET/JEE Physics & Chemistry step by step — clearing doubts, drilling the concepts, and checking you really understood before we move on. Let's begin.

units_dimensions.hook: You can multiply a speed by a time and get a distance — but you can never add a speed to a time. Why does physics forbid it?
units_dimensions.recall: What are the dimensions of force, and how do you know an equation is dimensionally wrong?
units_dimensions.answer: Force = [M L T^-2]. An equation is wrong if the two sides have different dimensions — only same-dimension quantities can be added or equated.

significant_figures.hook: A ruler says 2.5 cm and a vernier says 2.50 cm. Same number — but one is a stronger claim. What's the difference?
significant_figures.recall: How many significant figures are in 0.00405, and why?
significant_figures.answer: Three (4, 0, 5). Leading zeros are not significant; zeros between/after significant digits are.

error_analysis.hook: If a quantity is a product of two measured values, do their errors add, or do their percentage errors add?
error_analysis.recall: For Z = A·B, how do the relative (percentage) errors combine?
error_analysis.answer: For products/quotients the relative errors add: ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B. For powers, multiply by the exponent.

distance_vs_displacement.hook: You run one full lap of a 400 m track and stop where you started. Distance = 400 m. Displacement = ?
distance_vs_displacement.recall: State one situation where average speed is non-zero but average velocity is zero.
distance_vs_displacement.answer: Zero displacement (back to start). Any closed loop: distance travelled > 0 so average speed > 0, but net displacement = 0 so average velocity = 0.

velocity_acceleration.hook: A car slows down while still moving forward. Its velocity is positive — but its acceleration points backward. How can both be true?
velocity_acceleration.recall: Can a body have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant? Give an example.
velocity_acceleration.answer: Yes — at the top of a vertical throw velocity = 0 but acceleration = g downward. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, independent of velocity's current value.

equations_of_motion.hook: Three little equations describe every uniformly-accelerated motion in the universe. What's the one condition they all require?
equations_of_motion.recall: Write the three equations of motion for constant acceleration.
equations_of_motion.answer: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as. Valid only when acceleration a is constant.

projectile_motion.hook: A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time. Why?
projectile_motion.recall: In projectile motion, what happens to the horizontal and vertical velocity components over time?
projectile_motion.answer: Horizontal velocity stays constant (no horizontal force); vertical velocity changes due to g. The two motions are independent, so vertical fall time is the same as a dropped object.

newtons_first_law.hook: A spaceship far from any star keeps moving forever with its engines off. What law makes 'off' enough?
newtons_first_law.recall: State Newton's first law and define inertia.
newtons_first_law.answer: A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia is a body's resistance to change in its state of motion, measured by its mass.

newtons_second_law.hook: Push a shopping cart and a loaded truck with the same force. Same force — wildly different results. What equation captures why?
newtons_second_law.recall: State Newton's second law in terms of momentum, and its common form.
newtons_second_law.answer: F = dp/dt (net force = rate of change of momentum). For constant mass this becomes F = ma.

newtons_third_law.hook: The Earth pulls you down with your weight. By Newton's third law, you pull the Earth up with the SAME force. So why doesn't the Earth move?
newtons_third_law.recall: Action and reaction are equal and opposite — why do they never cancel each other out?
newtons_third_law.answer: They act on different bodies, so they never cancel. The Earth does accelerate, but its huge mass makes that acceleration negligibly small (a = F/m).

friction.hook: Static friction can be zero, or huge — it adjusts itself. What sets its maximum before something finally slips?
friction.recall: How does limiting static friction relate to the normal force, and how does kinetic friction compare?
friction.answer: f_s(max) = μ_s·N. Once moving, kinetic friction f_k = μ_k·N, and usually μ_k < μ_s (harder to start than to keep sliding).

work_done.hook: You hold a heavy bag still for an hour and get exhausted — but physics says you did zero work. How?
work_done.recall: Define work done by a force, and when it is zero despite a force acting.
work_done.answer: W = F·d·cosθ. Work is zero when displacement is zero, or when the force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°), e.g. carrying a bag horizontally or holding it still.

work_energy_theorem.hook: Forget the forces for a second — the total work done on a body equals just ONE thing about it. What?
work_energy_theorem.answer: The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − ½mu².

conservation_of_energy.hook: A pendulum swings up, stops, swings back — perfectly, forever, if there's no friction. What quantity is secretly staying constant?
conservation_of_energy.recall: For a freely falling body, how do KE and PE change while their sum stays fixed?
conservation_of_energy.answer: PE (mgh) converts to KE (½mv²) as it falls; total mechanical energy KE + PE stays constant when only conservative forces act.

power.hook: Two cranes lift the same load to the same height. Same work done — but one is 'more powerful.' What's the missing variable?
power.recall: Define power and give its relation to force and velocity.
power.answer: Power = work/time (rate of doing work). Instantaneously, P = F·v. SI unit: watt.

mole_concept.hook: Chemists count atoms — but atoms are far too small to count one by one. So they invented a 'dozen' for atoms. How big is it?
mole_concept.recall: What is one mole, and what is Avogadro's number?
mole_concept.answer: One mole is the amount containing as many entities as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12 — that is 6.022 × 10²³ (Avogadro's number).

molar_mass.hook: Why does 18 g of water and 44 g of CO₂ both contain exactly the same number of molecules?
molar_mass.recall: How do you find the number of moles from a given mass, and what is molar mass?
molar_mass.answer: moles = given mass / molar mass. Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams, numerically equal to the molecular/atomic mass in amu.

empirical_molecular_formula.hook: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆ and formaldehyde is CH₂O — different molecules, but the SAME simplest ratio. What's that ratio called?
empirical_molecular_formula.recall: What is the difference between empirical and molecular formula, and how are they related?
empirical_molecular_formula.answer: Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; molecular formula = actual number of atoms. Molecular = n × empirical, where n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.

limiting_reagent.hook: You have 10 bread slices and 3 cheese slices to make sandwiches. How many sandwiches — and what runs out first?
limiting_reagent.recall: What is the limiting reagent, and what determines the amount of product formed?
limiting_reagent.answer: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is fully consumed first; it caps how much product forms. The other reactant(s) are in excess.

bohr_model.hook: Classical physics says an orbiting electron should spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a second. Atoms don't collapse. What did Bohr forbid?
bohr_model.recall: What is quantised in Bohr's model, and what happens when an electron jumps between levels?
bohr_model.answer: Angular momentum is quantised (mvr = nh/2π), so only certain orbits are allowed. An electron absorbs energy to jump up and emits a photon (ΔE = hν) when it falls down.

quantum_numbers.hook: Four numbers pin down every electron in an atom like a postal address — and no two electrons can share all four. Why not?
quantum_numbers.recall: Name the four quantum numbers and state the Pauli exclusion principle.
quantum_numbers.answer: Principal (n), azimuthal (l), magnetic (m_l), spin (m_s). Pauli: no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers identical.

electronic_configuration.hook: Electrons could all pile into the lowest energy level — but they don't. Three rules decide where each one goes. Which rule fills lowest-energy orbitals first?
electronic_configuration.recall: State the Aufbau principle and Hund's rule.
electronic_configuration.answer: Aufbau: orbitals fill in order of increasing energy (lowest first). Hund's rule: within a subshell, each orbital gets one electron (parallel spins) before any is doubly filled.

periodic_law.hook: Mendeleev left GAPS in his table for elements nobody had discovered — and predicted their properties. What repeating pattern gave him the nerve?
periodic_law.answer: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number (not atomic mass) — repeating regularly as Z increases.

atomic_radius_trend.hook: Across a period you ADD electrons, yet atoms get SMALLER, not bigger. What overpowers the extra electrons?
atomic_radius_trend.recall: How does atomic radius change across a period and down a group, and why?
atomic_radius_trend.answer: Decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons in) and increases down a group (new shells added). Nuclear pull vs shell number is the tug-of-war.

ionization_energy.hook: Removing the first electron from sodium is easy; the second costs almost ten times more energy. What causes the sudden jump?
ionization_energy.recall: Define ionization energy and explain the large jump after a noble-gas configuration is reached.
ionization_energy.answer: Ionization energy is the energy to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. A huge jump appears when you start removing electrons from a stable, filled inner (noble-gas) shell.

electronegativity.hook: In a tug-of-war over shared electrons, fluorine always wins. What property measures who pulls hardest?
electronegativity.recall: What is electronegativity and how does it trend in the periodic table?
electronegativity.answer: Electronegativity is an atom's tendency to attract a shared electron pair in a bond. It increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative.

ionic_vs_covalent.hook: Sodium GIVES its electron away; two chlorine atoms SHARE. Same goal — a full shell — two different deals. What decides give vs share?
ionic_vs_covalent.recall: What is the key difference between ionic and covalent bonding, and what favours each?
ionic_vs_covalent.answer: Ionic = complete transfer of electrons (large electronegativity difference, metal + non-metal); covalent = sharing of electrons (small difference, non-metal + non-metal).

vsepr_shape.hook: Why is water bent at 104.5° and not a straight line? Something invisible is pushing the bonds apart.
vsepr_shape.recall: What is the central idea of VSEPR theory, and why is water bent?
vsepr_shape.answer: Electron pairs around a central atom repel and arrange to be as far apart as possible. Water has two bond pairs + two lone pairs; lone-pair repulsion pushes the O–H bonds to a bent 104.5° shape.

hybridization.hook: Carbon's four bonds in methane are all identical — but its s and p orbitals aren't. How does carbon make four equal bonds from unequal orbitals?
hybridization.recall: What is hybridization, and what is the hybridization and geometry of carbon in methane?
hybridization.answer: Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals to form new equivalent orbitals. Carbon in CH₄ is sp³ hybridised, giving four identical orbitals in a tetrahedral geometry (109.5°).
